rationale: A wins because it keeps the work inside the evidence fence and refuses the tempting fiction. Its strongest move is "Substack says its top creators earned $400M — the number it won't break down is the story," which turns the company's own disclosure into a real reporter question. B has useful instincts, but keeping "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" without a named writer is a customer story built on an empty chair, and saying "No current news signal was supplied" is just wrong when the update is a live launch.
gaps_in_A: "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" overstates what the update proves. The facts give a 10% subscription cut, not an explicit no-ads policy.
"its revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" is too hard. The update gives one take rate, not Substack's complete revenue stack.
A misses the defensive writer-distribution angle: what the video/feed push means for text-first writers who do not want to perform for a feed.
gaps_in_B: "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" should not be a kept angle without an actual named creator. Asking for the proof in the proof list does not make the story exist.
"No current news signal was supplied" contradicts the brief. Native video is launching now; that is the news signal.
"the writers who may lose out" is a sharp question but presented too close to fact. The update gives no evidence that text-first writers lose distribution.
"A reporter will multiply them" is risky math. The set knows the $400M gross/net ambiguity exists, but the angle still invites an implied revenue calculation before the inputs are clean.
